---
title: "Exercises — Crosslinking and fixation"
---

Pen and paper. Try each one before opening the **Hint**, and the hint before the
**Solution** — the reasoning is the point, not the answer. For the reagent questions, have a
supplier's crosslinker selection table in front of you; the columns you need are reactive
group, spacer-arm length, membrane permeability and cleavability.

# Part 1 — Choosing the chemistry

## E1. Pick the reagents, and say which property decides each

You want to map where a co-activator sits on human chromatin. The protein has no DNA-binding
domain: it is recruited to chromatin by a transcription factor. You will immunoprecipitate the
co-activator, and afterwards you need clean DNA for an ordinary library.

Choose the crosslinking reagents and the order in which they go in, and name the single
property of each that settles the choice.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
Two different bonds are needed: one holds the co-activator to the factor, one holds the
factor to the DNA. Which reagent can make each, and which of them has to come off again?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
A protein–protein reagent first, then formaldehyde. DSG (or another amine-to-amine ester)
joins the co-activator to the factor; the deciding property is the **spacer-arm length**,
because the two proteins are nowhere near one carbon apart. Formaldehyde then joins the factor
to the DNA; the deciding property is that its bridge is **one carbon long**, so what it
reports is contact, and that it is **reversible by heat**, so the DNA can be freed at the end.

The DSG bond is never reversed, and does not need to be: proteinase K digests the proteins it
joined. Both reagents must cross the plasma membrane, which rules out charged esters.
:::

## E2. The step that is easy to leave out

A protocol says: fix in 1% formaldehyde for 10 min at room temperature, add glycine to
125 mM, 5 min, then spin and wash. A student is short of time and goes straight from the
10 min to the spin, keeping everything cold from then on.

What has changed about the experiment, and would you expect the effect to be the same for
every sample in the batch?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
Formaldehyde is still present, so crosslinking continues through the spin and the wash. The
fixation time is no longer 10 min but 10 min plus however long the handling takes, and the
cold slows the reaction without stopping it. The effect is not uniform: the first tube in the
rack is handled faster than the last, so the batch now carries a fixation gradient that looks
like biological variation. The quench is what defines the end of the dose.
:::

## E3. Would formaldehyde answer this question?

You want to know which RNAs an RNA-binding protein touches directly in living cells. A
colleague points out that formaldehyde is cheap, works in any laboratory, and is reversible,
while UV needs a dedicated lamp. Give two reasons the two reagents do not answer the same
question.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
Think about reach, and about what a protein–protein bond does to an immunoprecipitation of a
ribonucleoprotein particle.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
First, reach: formaldehyde joins protein to protein as readily as protein to RNA, so an RNA
held by any other protein in the same particle is captured along with the one you pulled down.
The UV bond is zero-length and forms only between an RNA base and a side chain in contact with
it, so the footprint is the protein's own.

Second, washing: because the UV bond is covalent and specific to direct contact, the complex
can be washed under denaturing conditions, which removes everything held by affinity. A
formaldehyde-fixed particle cannot be washed that hard without losing the indirect bonds that
were the point of using it.

The reversibility that makes formaldehyde attractive is also what makes it the wrong reagent
here: the stub left by UV is what the CLIP readout measures.
:::

# Part 2 — What went wrong

## E4. Low yield and fragments that will not come down

A ChIP experiment gives very little DNA. The sheared chromatin runs as a smear centred well
above 1 kb, although the same sonicator settings gave 300 bp last month. The cells looked
healthy and the antibody is the one that worked before. The only change was that the
formaldehyde incubation ran for 30 min instead of 10 while the student was called away.

Explain the observation, and give two things to change.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
Over-fixation. More and longer crosslinking makes the chromatin a denser covalent network,
which resists shearing and is less soluble, so the material that does shear is a small and
biased fraction of the starting chromatin, and much of the sample never leaves the pellet.
Fragments that are too long also blur the signal, because the sequencer reads the ends.

Two changes: shorten the fixation and fix the time properly with a quench, or increase the
shearing energy or time to compensate. Both have a cost — the first captures fewer indirect
contacts, the second heats and fragments the sample further — and the usual approach is a
titration of fixation time against the fragment profile.
:::

## E5. A good antibody that gives no enrichment

An antibody detects a single clean band in a western blot of the same cells, but the ChIP
gives no enrichment over input at any locus, including a site confirmed by another method.
Give three explanations and say how you would tell them apart.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
A western blot is run on denatured, unfixed protein. Which step of the ChIP has no counterpart
in that experiment?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
1. **Epitope masking.** Formaldehyde has bridged a lysine inside the epitope, so the antibody
   no longer binds the fixed protein. A western blot cannot detect this, because it sees
   denatured, unfixed protein. Test it by repeating with a shorter fixation, or with an
   antibody raised against a different region.
2. **The protein is not held to the DNA.** If it contacts chromatin only through a partner, a
   single short-arm reagent captures nothing. Test it by adding a protein–protein crosslinker
   before the formaldehyde.
3. **The complex is lost before the pull-down.** Over-fixed chromatin stays in the pellet, so
   the target never enters the immunoprecipitation. Test it by blotting the input and the
   insoluble fraction for the target.

The three are distinguished by where the protein is, not by how much DNA comes out, so the
informative controls are blots of the fractions rather than more qPCR.
:::

## E6. Fewer genes per cell after fixation

The same cell line is profiled twice: once fresh, once after formaldehyde fixation and
permeabilisation. The fixed sample gives fewer genes detected per cell at the same sequencing
depth. Explain, and predict which transcripts lose the most.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
Crosslinked RNA is a poorer template: protein is still attached at the sites that were
crosslinked, and reverse transcription stops or is slowed at them. Fewer cDNA molecules are
made per transcript, so fewer distinct molecules are captured per cell.

The loss is not uniform. Transcripts that are heavily bound by protein, and long transcripts —
which carry more crosslinks per molecule, and for which a stop anywhere upstream of the
priming site costs the whole molecule — lose most. Lowly expressed genes fall below detection
first because they start with few molecules. The result is that fixation changes the
measured expression profile, not only its depth.
:::

## E7. Noise that does not dilute away

A proximity-ligation library has a high fraction of read pairs joining distant, unrelated
places. The usual explanation is ligation between ends from different complexes, so the
ligation is repeated at a tenfold greater dilution. The fraction barely moves.

What is the crosslinking-side explanation, and what would you change?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
Dilution only helps for joints made between two separate particles in solution.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
If the two pieces are already in one covalently joined particle, they ligate at any dilution,
because they never had to find each other. Two complexes crosslinked into one — by long
fixation, by aggregation, or by a long-arm reagent joining proteins that were not interacting
— produce junctions that look like contacts and behave like real signal under dilution.

What to change is upstream of the ligation: the fixation time and reagent, and whether the
reaction is run in intact nuclei rather than on released chromatin. The diagnostic is the
fraction of valid pairs as a function of fixation condition, not as a function of dilution.
:::

# Part 3 — Arithmetic, order and design

## E8. Is the quench in excess?

Formaldehyde has a relative molecular mass of 30. A 1% (w/v) solution is 10 g/L. The quench is
glycine at 125 mM. Work out the molarity of the formaldehyde, compare it with the glycine, and
say what this tells you about the quench.

Then estimate how many formaldehyde molecules are present per cell, taking a cell volume of
2 pL and assuming the interior reaches the same concentration as the medium. Compare with an
assumed 10^10^ protein molecules per cell.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
Molarity is grams per litre divided by the relative molecular mass. Avogadro's number is
6.0 × 10^23^.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
Formaldehyde: 10 / 30 = 0.33 M, that is 333 mM. Glycine at 125 mM is therefore about 0.4
equivalents — the quench is **below** the formaldehyde concentration, so it cannot consume all
of it on stoichiometry alone. It works because glycine is a small, fast-reacting free amine that competes for the
aldehyde, and because the wash that follows removes what is left; the quench is not a
stoichiometric one.
This is why protocols differ in glycine concentration and in whether they rely on the wash,
and why leaving out the quench altogether is a larger change than it looks.

Per cell: 0.33 mol/L × 2 × 10^−12^ L = 6.6 × 10^−13^ mol, times 6.0 × 10^23^ = about
4 × 10^11^ molecules. Against 10^10^ protein molecules that is roughly 40 formaldehyde
molecules per protein. The reagent is nowhere near limiting: what limits crosslinking is how
often two amines are in contact and how long you leave it, not how much formaldehyde you add.
:::

## E9. Why is the CLIP adapter ligated while the protein is still there?

In CLIP the 3′ adapter is ligated to the RNA while the protein–RNA complex is still bound to
the beads, before the protease. Ligating to clean, deproteinised RNA would be easier. Why is
it not done that way?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
Because there is no point at which the RNA is both clean and intact. The UV bond cannot be
reversed, so the protein can only be removed by digesting it, and that leaves a peptide stub
on the RNA whatever you do. Meanwhile the complex on the beads is the only thing holding the
footprint through the stringent washes: release it and the short RNA is lost with everything
else.

Ligating on the beads also means the adapter is attached before the RNA is eluted, so every
molecule that survives the washes carries a handle. The sequence of operations follows from a
bond that will not come off.
:::

## E10. Design: archival tissue, protein–DNA binding

You are given formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded human tumour blocks and asked to map where a
transcription factor binds. A tethered-enzyme method such as CUT&RUN works on unfixed,
permeabilised cells, and you have none.

List the properties the method you use must have, given the material, and say which step of
the crosslinking block each property comes from.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
Go through the block in order: what was done to the sample, what state it is in now, and what
each later step needs from it.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
- **It must work on crosslinked chromatin.** The sample was fixed for hours to days, not
  minutes, so the network is dense. That rules out methods that need native, unfixed chromatin
  for the enzyme or for the antibody, and it means shearing will be hard: the fragmentation
  step has to be chosen for over-fixed material.
- **The antibody must bind a fixed epitope.** Fixation is already done and cannot be titrated,
  so epitope masking is a property of the sample. An antibody validated on fixed material is a
  requirement rather than a preference.
- **It must include a reversal.** The bonds are there and nothing downstream can proceed
  through them, so heat and protease are not optional, and the long fixation means a longer
  reversal.
- **It must tolerate damaged DNA.** The same heat that reverses the crosslinks, plus years in
  a block, leaves short, nicked, deaminated fragments. The library chemistry has to accept
  short inserts and ragged ends.

The exercise is not to name a protocol but to notice that the first step of the block was
taken by someone else, years ago, and every later step inherits it.
:::

# Self-check

1. What two chemical groups does formaldehyde join, and how long is the bridge?
2. Why is a second, longer-armed reagent used, and why does it not need reversing?
3. What makes the UV bond zero-length, and what is left on the RNA after proteinase K?
4. Which two steps reverse a formaldehyde crosslink, in which order, and what does each do?
5. Name the two opposite requirements that permeabilisation has to satisfy.
6. Give one failure mode that gets worse with more crosslinking and one that gets worse with
   less.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answers
1. Two primary amines — lysine side chains, and the exocyclic amino groups of the bases — so
   protein–protein and protein–nucleic-acid. The bridge is a single carbon, about 2.3 Å.
2. To hold a protein that touches the nucleic acid only through a partner, which a one-carbon
   bridge cannot span. It needs no reversal because the proteins it joined are digested by
   proteinase K at the end.
3. The base itself absorbs the photon and bonds directly to a side chain already in contact
   with it, with no linker in between. Proteinase K leaves a peptide stub on the crosslinked
   nucleotide.
4. Heat, typically 65 °C overnight, hydrolyses the methylene bridge and releases the protein
   from the nucleic acid; proteinase K then digests the protein itself. Heat first.
5. Letting enzymes, antibodies and oligonucleotides in, while keeping the cell's own molecules
   from diffusing out.
6. Worse with more: epitope masking, chromatin that will not shear, lost accessibility,
   chimeric complexes. Worse with less: the association is lost during lysis and washing, so
   there is nothing left to pull down.
:::
